The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 7 September 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

A decision record without a stated falsifier is a press release. The one field that turns it into judgment is "what would prove this wrong, by when". A good falsifier names a measure, a threshold, a date and an observer, which turns a decision into a prediction that someone other than the author can grade. It is also the field that reveals, at the moment of decision, whether the people agreeing actually agree.

A rationale is an argument, and arguments do not expire. Most decision templates ask for context, options, the choice and the rationale. Every one of those can be written persuasively after the fact, and none of them can be checked. The decision record explainer calls the remedy the expected outcome; this piece is about writing it well.

A falsifier does what a rationale cannot. "If renewal rates in this segment fall below 85% within two quarters, this pricing change was wrong." It names a measure, a threshold and a date, and someone other than the author can observe it. It turns a decision into a prediction, and predictions can be graded.

Why predictions beat rationales

The strongest evidence that explicit, graded predictions improve judgment comes from forecasting research. In the geopolitical forecasting tournament reported by Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock and colleagues in Psychological Science in 2014, forecasters made explicit probability judgments that were scored against what happened. Three interventions improved both calibration and resolution: training in probabilistic reasoning, teaming so forecasters could share the reasoning behind their beliefs, and tracking the best performers into elite teams.

None of that is possible with a rationale. A business decision is not a geopolitical forecast, and most firms will never score themselves the way a tournament does. The transferable lesson is narrower: judgment improves when a claim is stated in a form that the world can contradict, and when someone checks.

Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein reached a related conclusion from opposite directions. In their 2009 paper on intuitive expertise they argued that judging whether to trust an expert's intuition depends on how predictable the environment is and whether the expert has had the chance to learn its regularities. In a 2010 interview with McKinsey Quarterly, Klein added feedback as the second condition. A falsifier is how an organisation manufactures feedback for decisions that would otherwise never get any.

Anatomy of a good falsifier

Four parts, all required:

PartWhat it isWeak versionWhy the weak version fails
MeasureA quantity or an observable event, not a feeling"If it doesn't work out"No measure
ThresholdThe level at which you would say the decision was wrong"If adoption is disappointing"No threshold
DateWhen you will look"If we don't see results"No date
ObserverWho checks, and from what sourceLeft blankNobody looks

Weak falsifiers are not falsifiers. They are permission to decide later what the decision meant.

Some examples across decision classes:

Decision classFalsifier
Credit"If the leverage ratio exceeds 5.5x at the next two reporting dates, the approval assumptions failed."
Pricing"If win rate in the mid-market band drops more than 8 points over the next 40 opportunities, the new price is wrong."
Partnership"If the partner has not sourced three qualified introductions by end of Q2, the channel thesis is wrong."
Hiring"If the new team lead has not run the weekly review independently by month four, the internal promotion was the wrong call."

Notice that the pricing example counts opportunities rather than weeks. Where volume is low, a count-based date stops the check arriving before there is enough evidence to read. Our piece on campaign tests that reach a decision applies the same logic to marketing experiments.

The falsifier as an alignment test

Writing a falsifier does work at the moment of decision. It forces each person to state what they are actually betting on. Two people who agreed on the choice often write different falsifiers, because they agreed on what to do but not on why. One supports the price change because it will lift margin; the other because it will screen out bad-fit customers. Those are different bets with different failure signals.

That disagreement is worth more than the agreement. Surfacing it before the decision is cheaper than discovering it in the post-mortem. Klein's premortem works on the same principle: the team imagines the project has already failed and lists why. Klein cites 1989 research by Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington finding that this kind of prospective hindsight "increases the ability to correctly identify reasons for future outcomes by 30%". Kahneman called the premortem "a low-cost, high-payoff kind of thing". A falsifier is a premortem reduced to one line and attached to the record.

The order matters. Ask each decision-maker to write their own falsifier before discussion, then compare. Written after discussion, falsifiers converge on whoever spoke first. Our piece Dissent is the data you are throwing away makes the wider case for recording the disagreement.

Two people who agree on a choice often write different falsifiers. They agreed on what to do, not on why.

What happens when one triggers

Record it as triggered. Then make one of three explicit choices: reverse the decision, hold it with a new and recorded reason, or accept the loss and close the record. What must never happen is a quiet edit of the threshold. Moving the goalposts is sometimes legitimate, but it is a new decision, and it should be recorded as a supersession with its own reason, as set out in Supersede, never overwrite.

The outcome itself goes back to the same record. Our explainer on outcome write-back covers the mechanics.

Calibrating the falsifiers themselves

Track the share of decisions whose falsifiers trigger. If it is close to zero, the falsifiers are too safe and are measuring nothing. If it is very high, either the decisions are too bold or the thresholds too tight. Somewhere in between, you are learning. There is no published benchmark for the right share in business decisions; the useful signal is the trend in your own record and whether people can explain it. Calibration is the honest learning signal covers how to read that trend.

Report monthlyWhat it shows
Share of material decisions with a valid falsifierWhether the habit is holding
Share checked on or before the dateWhether observers are doing their part
Share triggeredWhether thresholds are honest
Share triggered and quietly editedWhether goalposts are moving

In practice

Make measure, threshold, date and observer required on every material decision. Ask each decision-maker to write their own falsifier before discussion, then compare. Put the check date in the observer's calendar, not just the record.

Report the share with valid falsifiers, the share reviewed on time, and the share triggered.

What would prove this wrong: decisions recorded with falsifiers showing no better follow-through, learning or later outcomes than decisions recorded without them. Then the field is ritual.

lowob takeaways

  • Four parts, all required. Measure, threshold, date and observer.
  • Write them before discussion. Different falsifiers reveal different bets.
  • Never move the threshold quietly. A changed threshold is a new decision with its own record.
  • Watch the trigger rate. Near zero means the falsifiers are too safe.

Common questions

What is a falsifier in a decision record?

A statement of what would prove the decision wrong, by when. It names a measure, a threshold, a date and an observer, which turns a decision into a prediction that can be graded.

How do I write a good falsifier for a business decision?

Include a measure that is a quantity or observable event, a threshold at which the decision is wrong, a date or case count when you will look, and who checks from what source. For example: if renewal rates in this segment fall below 85% within two quarters, this pricing change was wrong.

What is the difference between a falsifier and a premortem?

A premortem asks a team to imagine a decision has failed and list why. A falsifier states, in one line attached to the record, the observable result that would show it failed, so it can be checked later.

What should happen when a decision's falsifier is triggered?

Record it as triggered, then explicitly reverse the decision, hold it with a new recorded reason, or accept the loss and close the record. Changing the threshold is a new decision and should be recorded as a supersession.

Sources and notes

  • Mellers et al., Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament, Psychological Science, 2014. Academic study; geopolitical questions, not business decisions.
  • Gary Klein, Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review, September 2007. Practitioner article; the 30% figure is from 1989 research it cites. Copy hosted by a third party.
  • Kahneman and Klein, Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree, American Psychologist 64(6), 2009. Academic review; abstract only.
  • McKinsey Quarterly, Strategic decisions: When can you trust your gut?, 1 March 2010. Interview with Kahneman and Klein; opinion, not new data.
  • The four-part falsifier, the alignment test and the trigger-rate report are lowob's working method.

At your next material decision, ask each person to write their own falsifier before discussion, with a measure, threshold, date and observer. Compare them before you decide, and put the check date in the observer's calendar.
